Design patterns
What is a design pattern?
A general, reusable solution to a common problem in a given context.
Part
What it tells us
Name & type
A shared vocabulary
Problem
When the pattern is useful: the problem and its context
Solution
The classes, their relations and responsibilities
Consequences
The results and tradeoffs of using it
Variants
Similar designs built on the same idea
Part 1
Singleton
Exactly one instance, and everyone gets the same one.
Part 1 · Singleton
Two screens, two dispatchers
// OrderService DeliveryDispatcher d =     new DeliveryDispatcher(); d.assign(order1); // RestaurantPanel DeliveryDispatcher d =     new DeliveryDispatcher(); d.assign(order2);
1
Each dispatcher has its own view of the fleet
2
Both see courier #17 as available
3
Courier #17 gets two orders at once
Some objects must exist exactly once, so that every part of the app sees the same state.
Part 1 · Singleton
The fix: one instance, one access point
public class DeliveryDispatcher {     protected static DeliveryDispatcher             instance = null;     protected DeliveryDispatcher() { }     public static DeliveryDispatcher theInstance() {         if (instance == null)             instance = new DeliveryDispatcher();         return instance;     } }
// everywhere DeliveryDispatcher.theInstance().assign(order);
1 · Hidden constructor
protected, so no one outside can call new
2 · Static field
Holds the one instance
3 · Static accessor
Creates it on the first call, then always returns it
Part 1 · Singleton
Singleton in a class diagram
«Singleton»
DeliveryDispatcher
- instance : DeliveryDispatcher
# DeliveryDispatcher() + theInstance() : DeliveryDispatcher + assign(o : Order) : void
«Singleton» stereotype on the class
Underlined = static, belongs to the class
# constructor: subclasses only
Clients call theInstance(), never new
Part 1 · Singleton
Two threads, one null check
Without a lock
Thread A
Thread B
instance == null ✔
instance == null ✔
new Dispatcher()
new Dispatcher()
Two dispatchers: the exact bug we tried to prevent.
Fix
public static synchronized DeliveryDispatcher theInstance() {     if (instance == null)         instance = new DeliveryDispatcher();     return instance; }
synchronized: only one thread runs the method at a time.
Part 1 · Singleton variants
Eager initialization
public class OrderIdGenerator {     private static final OrderIdGenerator         instance = new OrderIdGenerator();     private int next = 1000;     private OrderIdGenerator() { }     public static OrderIdGenerator getInstance() {         return instance;     }     public synchronized int nextId() {         return next++;     } }
Lazy
Eager
Created
On the first call
When the class loads
Safe creation
Needs synchronized
For free
Good for
Expensive, needs setup first
Cheap, no dependencies
Example
DeliveryDispatcher: loads the fleet from the DB
OrderIdGenerator: just a counter
Part 1 · Singleton variants
A fixed number of instances
public class PaymentConnection {     private static final int MAX = 3;     private static int next = 0;     private static PaymentConnection[] pool =         new PaymentConnection[MAX];     private PaymentConnection() { }     public static PaymentConnection theInstance() {         if (pool[next] == null)             pool[next] = new PaymentConnection();         PaymentConnection result = pool[next];         next = (next + 1) % MAX;         return result;     } }
The need
The payment provider allows only 3 open connections.
Round robin
Calls get connection 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2…
Never a fourth
Same idea as Singleton, with N instead of 1.
Part 1 · Singleton variants
Singleton with inheritance
One payment gateway for the whole app: Stripe or PayPal, chosen once.
public abstract class PaymentGateway {     protected static PaymentGateway instance;     public static PaymentGateway theInstance() {         assert instance != null             : "No gateway chosen";         return instance;     }     public abstract void charge(Order o); }
public class StripeGateway         extends PaymentGateway {     protected StripeGateway() { }     public static PaymentGateway theInstance() {         if (instance == null)             instance = new StripeGateway();         return instance;     }     public void charge(Order o) { ... } }
Part 1 · Singleton variants
One line decides the type
// main: the ONLY place that knows the concrete class StripeGateway.theInstance(); // everywhere else PaymentGateway.theInstance().charge(order);
First caller wins
A later PayPalGateway.theInstance() still returns the Stripe object. They share one field.
Hidden, not overridden
Static methods aren’t overridden in Java. That’s why there’s no @Override.
assert needs -ea
Without the -ea flag the check is skipped, and you just get null.
Part 1 · Singleton
Is Singleton an antipattern?
A global variable
Any class can reach it. Dependencies are hidden.
Hard to test
Can’t swap in a mock dispatcher. State leaks between tests.
Bends SRP
The class does its job and also polices its own instance count.
Hard to undo
A dispatcher per city? Change every theInstance() call.
The problem is misuse. DeliveryDispatcher really must be one. A shopping Cart must not.
Part 2
Factory
Move the decision of which class to create out of the code that uses it.
Part 2 · Factory
Three patterns called “Factory”
Pattern
Idea
Who picks the concrete class
Factory class
A separate class that creates objects
The factory, with a switch
Factory method
An abstract create method in the base class
The subclass that overrides it
Abstract factory
A factory for a whole family of objects
The concrete factory subclass
In all three, the client works with an interface and never writes new for a concrete class.
Part 2 · Factory class
A new courier signs up
// DeliveryDispatcher public void onboard(String type, CourierInfo i) {     Courier c;     if (type.equals("BIKE"))         c = new BikeCourier(i);     else if (type.equals("CAR"))         c = new CarCourier(i);     itsFleet.add(c); }
Knows every courier class
The dispatcher depends on BikeCourier, CarCourier, and every future type.
Then drones arrive
Open the dispatcher and add a branch. Same edit in every class that creates couriers.
Part 2 · Factory class
The fix: a CourierFactory
CourierFactory
public class CourierFactory {     public Courier create(String type,                           CourierInfo i) {         switch (type) {             case "BIKE":  return new BikeCourier(i);             case "CAR":   return new CarCourier(i);             case "DRONE": return new DroneCourier(i);         }         return null;     } }
DeliveryDispatcher
void onboard(String type,              CourierInfo i) {     itsFleet.add(         factory.create(type, i)); }
Drones added. The dispatcher didn’t change.
Part 2 · Factory class
What the factory bought us
Dispatcher closed
It only knows Courier. Drones didn’t touch it. (DIP, OCP)
Creation in one place
Validation, defaults, IDs: written once, not in every client. (SRP)
The factory still changes
Every new type adds a case. The factory itself can break OCP.
The factory is often a Singleton too: one CourierFactory, used everywhere.
Part 2 · Factory method
Let the subclass decide
The base class runs the algorithm. A subclass decides which object it needs.
Base class
The shared algorithm, plus an abstract createX() that returns an interface.
Each subclass
Overrides createX() and returns its own concrete class.
Fits when the object is born inside the algorithm: a fresh one every time it runs.
Part 2 · Factory method
Every delivery gets its own tracking
public abstract class DeliveryService {     public void startDelivery(Order o,                               Courier c) {         TrackingSession t =             createTracking(c);         t.start();         o.getCustomer().showLiveMap(t);         c.deliver(o);     }     protected abstract TrackingSession             createTracking(Courier c); }
class BikeDeliveryService         extends DeliveryService {     protected TrackingSession             createTracking(Courier c) {         return new PhoneGpsTracking(c);     } } class DroneDeliveryService         extends DeliveryService {     protected TrackingSession             createTracking(Courier c) {         return new DroneTelemetry(c);     } }
Part 2 · Factory method
Factory method: the tradeoff
Drones = one subclass
startDelivery() is never edited. No switch anywhere. (OCP)
Base sees abstractions
Only TrackingSession, never PhoneGpsTracking. (DIP)
Two jobs per subclass
Each subclass does its logic and creates products. With many products, it can break SRP.
Factory class
Factory method
New type means
A new case in the switch
A new subclass
Risk
Breaks OCP
Breaks SRP

Without it: mixed families
// OrderService, US branch gateway  = new DollarGateway(); notifier = new HebrewSms(); tax      = new IsraelVat();
Nothing stops this: OrderService picks each class on its own.

Part 3 · Abstract factory
One factory per market
public abstract class MarketFactory {     public abstract PaymentGateway             createGateway();     public abstract Notifier             createNotifier();     public abstract TaxCalculator             createTax(); }
Factory class: creation lives in its own object (SRP)
Factory methods: each market overrides them (OCP)
public class IsraelFactory         extends MarketFactory {     public PaymentGateway createGateway() {         return new ShekelGateway();     }     public Notifier createNotifier() {         return new HebrewSms();     }     public TaxCalculator createTax() {         return new IsraelVat();     } }
UsFactory: same shape, US products.
Part 3 · Abstract factory
One market, chosen once
public abstract class MarketFactory {     protected static MarketFactory theInstance;     public static MarketFactory theFactory() {         assert theInstance != null;         return theInstance;     }     // + the three abstract create methods }
public class IsraelFactory         extends MarketFactory {     protected IsraelFactory() { }     public static MarketFactory theFactory() {         if (theInstance == null)             theInstance = new IsraelFactory();         return theInstance;     } }
Same trick as PaymentGateway: a singleton with inheritance. The first theFactory() call fixes the market.
Part 3 · Abstract factory
The client never sees a market
public class OrderService {     public OrderService() {         MarketFactory f = MarketFactory.theFactory();         gateway  = f.createGateway();         notifier = f.createNotifier();         tax      = f.createTax();     } } // main: the one line that picks the market IsraelFactory.theFactory(); OrderService service = new OrderService();
No mixing
Every product comes from the same factory object.
US launch
Add UsFactory and its products. Change one line in main.
Part 3 · Abstract factory
Why not theFactory(int id)?
The tempting version
public abstract class MarketFactory {     public static MarketFactory theFactory(int id) {         if (theInstance == null) {             if (id == 0) theInstance = new IsraelFactory();             else         theInstance = new UsFactory();         }         return theInstance;     } }
MarketFactory depends on its own children
OrderService depends on MarketFactory
So OrderService depends on every market
With the inheritance trick, only main knows a concrete factory

theFactory(int id)
OrderService

Singleton with inheritance
OrderService
MarketFactory

Arrow = “mentions by name.” Dependencies chain: on the left, OrderService depends on every market. On the right, every arrow points at the abstraction, and only main names a concrete factory.
